analysis.note: Deictic pronoun referring to ātmā; sandhi before sanātanaḥ gives printed -ṃ.
Predicate adjective of ātmā; interpreted by Śaṅkara as ancient/enduring and unproduced from any cause.

justifications.decision: The repeated masculine nominative predicates and pronouns are taken as predications of the ātmā, not of a body or another unspecified object. Śaṅkara explicitly supplies ātmā as the referent.
options_considered: ayam as a merely unspecified deictic, “this thing”
ayam as the embodied physical person/body
ayam as the ātman continuing from the preceding discussion

justifications.decision: The forms are read passively as impossibility predicates, not as active qualities. Śaṅkara frames the point as the incapacity of destructive agents to destroy the ātmā.
options_considered: active/descriptive meanings such as “not drying”
material-property language about a physical substance
passive impossibility: “not to be cut/burned/wetted/dried”
justifications.chosen: The negative gerundives mean that the Self cannot be cut, burned, moistened, or dried.

evidence.translation: they are not able to destroy this ātman

justifications.decision: The sequence is not read as literal travel everywhere. Śaṅkara makes all-pervasion follow from eternality: because it is eternal, it is sarvagata.
options_considered: sarva-gata as “gone everywhere” through motion
sarva-gata as all-pervading/omnipresent predication of the eternal ātman

evidence.translation: because it is eternal, it is all-pervading

justifications.decision: Although sthāṇu can denote a stump, post, or pillar, Śaṅkara glosses the intended sense as sthira, “stable/firm.” The translation therefore avoids a literal noun such as “post.”
options_considered: sthāṇuḥ as the noun “post/stump/pillar”
sthāṇuḥ as an adjective, “stable, firm”

evidence.quote: sarva-gatatvāt sthāṇur iva, sthira ity etat |
evidence.translation: because it is all-pervading, like a sthāṇu; that is, stable

justifications.decision: The word is taken as a predicate of the ātmā following from stability, not as the noun “mountain.”
options_considered: acalaḥ as the noun “mountain”
acalaḥ as the adjective “immovable, unmoving”

evidence.translation: because of stability, this ātman is immovable

justifications.decision: Śaṅkara glosses sanātana as cirantana and denies origination from any cause. Hence the translation uses “primordial” rather than merely “old.” The supplied line’s final abhinava ity arthaḥ is understood under the preceding negation, not as an assertion that the Self is “new.”
options_considered: sanātana as merely “old/ancient”
sanātana as “everlasting” without reference to non-origination
sanātana as primordial/beginningless, unproduced from any cause

evidence.quote: ataḥ sanātanaś cirantanaḥ, na kāraṇāt kutaścin niṣpannaḥ
evidence.translation: therefore sanātana means ancient/enduring, not produced from any cause whatsoever

justifications.decision: The verse’s apparent repetition is not flattened away as careless redundancy. Śaṅkara says some repetition is verbal and some semantic, because the ātman is difficult to understand and is being taught again in different words.
options_considered: compressing the verse into a single generic “it is indestructible”
treating the repetitions as accidental redundancy
preserving the pedagogical series of restatements
justifications.chosen: The repeated predicates are intentional restatement of the ātman’s eternality and changelessness.

evidence.translation: the eternality and changelessness of the ātman have been stated

evidence.quote: kiṃcic chabdataḥ punaruktam, kiṃcid arthataḥ iti |
evidence.translation: some is repeated verbally, some in meaning

evidence.quote: durbodhatvāt ātma-vastunaḥ punaḥ punaḥ prasaṅgam āpādya śabdāntareṇa tad eva vastu nirūpayati bhagavān vāsudevaḥ
evidence.translation: because the reality that is the ātman is hard to understand, Bhagavān Vāsudeva repeatedly brings that very reality into discussion and expounds it in other words

justifications.decision: The commentary is silent on a special restrictive scope for eva. On grammar and MW s.v. eva, 232,2, I take it as an emphatic particle strengthening aśoṣya, with ca as the connective “and.”
options_considered: exclusive “only” with aśoṣya
emphatic “indeed” with connective ca

translation: This Self (ātman) cannot be cut; this Self cannot be burned; it cannot be moistened, and indeed cannot be dried. Eternal (nitya), all-pervading (sarvagata), stable (sthāṇu), immovable (acala)—this Self is primordial (sanātana).
one_shot_delta: A commentary-blind translation might render sthāṇuḥ literally as “a post/stump”; Śaṅkara’s sthira gloss makes “stable/firm” the intended sense.
It might take sarva-gataḥ as motion-language, “gone everywhere”; Śaṅkara’s nityatvāt sarvagataḥ points to all-pervasion of the eternal Self.
It might translate sanātanaḥ simply as “old” or repeat “eternal”; Śaṅkara adds that the Self is not produced from any cause, so “primordial/beginningless” is intended.
It might flatten the verse as redundant. Śaṅkara says the repetitions are deliberate restatements of the hard-to-grasp ātman in other words.
analyzer_disagreements: ByT5 represented sarva_gataḥ as sarva_Cp + gataḥ_gam_SNPaM; for this apparatus I analyze the printed hyphenated word as one inflected tatpuruṣa compound stem sarvagata, Pum Prathama Eka. The verifier’s unsupported relation log is treated as a limitation rather than a reason to abandon the compound analysis.
ByT5 gave the privative forms only as unanalyzed adjectival stems; I retain its case/number/gender but add traditional nañ-tatpuruṣa vigrahas for acchedya, adāhya, akledya, aśoṣya, and acala.
open_questions: Line 1 in the supplied plaintext reads asyādīni, which looks corrupt or typo-like in context; the interpretation above does not depend on that token.
Line 5’s abhinava ity arthaḥ is printed without an explicit second na; I understand it elliptically under the preceding negation as “not new/newly produced,” consistent with sanātanaś cirantanaḥ.
mula: acchedyo 'yam adāhyo 'yam akledyo 'śoṣya eva ca | nityaḥ sarva-gataḥ sthāṇur acalo 'yaṃ sanātanaḥ
commentary_lines: yasmāt anyonya-nāśa-hetu-bhūtāni enam ātmānaṃ nāśayituṃ notsahante asyādīni tasmāt nityaḥ |
sarva-gatatvāt sthāṇur iva, sthira ity etat |
ataḥ sanātanaś cirantanaḥ, na kāraṇāt kutaścin niṣpannaḥ, abhinava ity arthaḥ |
naiteṣāṃ lokānāṃ paunaruktyaṃ codanīyam, yataḥ ekenaiva lokān ātmanaḥ nityatvam avikriyatvaṃ coktam na jāyate mriyate vā ity ādinā |
tatra yad eva ātma-viṣayaṃ kiṃcid ucyate, tad etasmāt lokārthān nātiricyate |
kiṃcic chabdataḥ punaruktam, kiṃcid arthataḥ iti |

durbodhatvāt ātma-vastunaḥ punaḥ punaḥ prasaṅgam āpādya śabdāntareṇa tad eva vastu nirūpayati bhagavān vāsudevaḥ kathaṃ nu nāma saṃsāriṇām asaṃsāritva-buddhi-gocaratām āpannaṃ sat avyaktaṃ tattvaṃ saṃsāra-nivṛttaye syāt iti ||bhgs_2.24||
